title: Passwords, MFA and Password Managers
oneLiner: Why length beats complexity, how long a password really lasts against online and offline attacks, how to generate good ones, and which kinds of multi-factor authentication stop phishing.
keyTakeaway: Use a password manager so every account gets a long, random, unique password, and remember only a few passphrases of several random words. Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere, and prefer passkeys or security keys, which phishing can't relay. Never approve a sign-in prompt you didn't start.
explanation:
Attackers rarely guess passwords one at a time at a login page; that's slow and gets accounts locked. They use lists. Credential stuffing tries email and password pairs leaked from other sites, which works because people reuse passwords. Password spraying tries a few very common passwords against many accounts. And when a site's password database is stolen, offline cracking tests billions of guesses a second against the hashes, where a fast unsalted hash like MD5 falls quickly and a slow, salted one like bcrypt holds out far longer.

Strength comes from randomness and length, not from swapping a for @. A password's strength is measured in bits of entropy: each bit doubles the number of guesses needed, but only if the choice was truly random. Summer2026! looks complex yet follows the first pattern cracking tools try. Several random words, a passphrase, are long, random and easy to type. A password manager goes further: it generates and remembers a different random password for every site, and it won't fill one in on a lookalike domain, which quietly protects against phishing.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second proof besides the password: something you have (a phone, a security key) or something you are (a fingerprint). It stops credential stuffing almost completely. Not all MFA is equal, though. SMS codes, authenticator app codes (TOTP, time-based one-time passwords) and push approvals can be phished: a fake login page asks for the code and relays it within seconds, and attackers spam push prompts hoping you'll tap Approve (MFA fatigue). Passkeys and FIDO2 security keys are phishing-resistant because they're cryptographically bound to the real site's domain. Test some passwords below, generate better ones, and compare MFA methods.
